{{Short description|Method to avoid singularities in classical mechanics}}
In [[mathematical physics]], the '''Ligon–Schaaf regularization''' is a method to describe the [[Singularity (mathematics)|singularities]] of collisions in the [[Kepler problem]] using the '''Ligon–Schaaf (regularization) map'''. Both are named after Thomas Ligon and Manfred Schaaf, who introduced them in 1976. (Thomas Ligon wrote his [[Diploma thesis|Diploma Thesis,]] now Master Thesis, about them under Manfred Schaaf's supervision.) Compared to other methods of regularization, the Ligon–Schaaf regularization possesses special properties like not transforming time or being able to transform all negative energy levels together. (The related [[Moser regularization]] requires a fixed energy.)

== Ligon–Schaaf map ==
Let <math>
E\colon T^*(\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\})\rightarrow\mathbb{R},
(q,p)\mapsto\frac{1}{2}|p|^2-\frac{1}{|q|}
</math> the [[Hamilton function]] ([[energy]]) of the [[Kepler problem]]. Let furthermore:<ref name=":1">Frauenfelder & van Koert 2018, p. 53-54</ref>

: <math>
u(q,p)
:=\left(\sqrt{-2E(q,p)}|q|p,|p|^2|q|-1\right)
\in\mathbb{R}^3;
</math>
: <math>
v(q,p)
:=\left(|q|^{-1}q-\langle q,p\rangle,\sqrt{-2E(q,p)}\langle q,p\rangle\right)
\in\mathbb{R}^3;
</math>
: <math>
\phi(q,p)
:=\sqrt{-2E(q,p)}\langle q,p\rangle.
</math>

The Ligon–Schaaf map <math>
\Phi\colon T^*(\mathbb{R}^2\setminus\{0\})\supset E^{-1}((-\infty,0])\rightarrow T^*S^2\setminus S^2
</math> is then given by:<ref name=":1" />

: <math>
\Phi(q,p)
:=\left(\cos(\phi)u+\sin(\phi)v,\sin(\phi)u-\cos(\phi)v\right)
\in T^*S^2\subset T^*\mathbb{R}^3\cong \mathbb{R}^3\times\mathbb{R}^3.
</math>

== Properties ==

* <math>u</math> and <math>v</math> are [[Orthonormality|orthonormal]], hence <math>\langle u,v\rangle=0</math>, <math>|u|=1</math> und <math>|v|=1</math>.<ref>Ligon 2018, Eq. (30) - (32)</ref><ref>Frauenfelder & van Koert 2018, Lemma 4.3.1</ref> Hence the Ligon–Schaaf map indeed maps to the subset <math>T^*S^2\subset T^*\mathbb{R}^3\cong \mathbb{R}^3\times\mathbb{R}^3</math> and is therefore [[Well-defined expression|well-defined]].
* The Ligon–Schaaf map <math>\Phi</math> is a [[symplectomorphism]].<ref>Frauenfelder & van Koert 2018, Lemma 4.3.2</ref>
* With the Delaunay Hamiltonian <math>
D\colon T^*S^2\setminus S^2\rightarrow\mathbb{R},
y\mapsto -\frac{1}{2y^2}
</math>, one has:<ref>Ligon 2018, Eq. (40)</ref><ref>Frauenfelder & van Koert 2018, S. 53-54</ref>
*: <math>
E=D\circ\Phi.
</math>
* With the [[cross product]] <math>
\mu\colon T^*S^2\setminus S^2\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^3,
(x,y)\mapsto x\times y
</math>, the [[Runge–Lenz vector]] <math>
A
</math> and [[angular momentum]] <math>
L
</math>:<ref>Ligon 2018, Eq. (38) - (39)</ref><ref>Frauenfelder & van Koert 2018, S. 53-54</ref>
*: <math>
\left(\frac{(A_2,-A_1))}{\sqrt{-2E}},L\right)=\mu\circ\Phi.
</math>
